synopsis: Semantic replay bypasses perception and feeds real decision, warning and braking logic with recorded or ground-truth object lists in common coordinates plus machine state; it can operate open loop or closed loop, with lists regenerated as the virtual machine slows [f5253, f5254, f13457, f13459]. It tests thresholds, threat assessment, warning stages and brake-request rules independently of sensor modality, but cannot prove perception and can hide latency, occlusion, false detections and range or classification errors; reported off-road maturity is medium for logic and absent for perception [f5256, f13463, f5686]. It is described as the cheapest way to sweep large scenario sets, supporting millions of braking-logic combinations through highly parallel CPU workloads on commodity servers without rendering or ray tracing [f13460, f9322, f16181]. Recording only object lists limits future replay to downstream software and prevents testing new perception algorithms, sensor models or mounting positions; where suppliers expose only object lists, validating a phenomenological model at that interface is considered more defensible than inventing a raw-signal model [f5628, f12990, f4868]. The recommended progression starts SIL with semantic inputs before adding realistic sensor errors, and pairs semantic replay with end-to-end replay when warning logic changes but perception remains unchanged: semantic coverage and expensive raw-sensor testing are complementary, rather than one approach dominating [f13466, f5497, f5779].
